title: The Win-Rate Wobble

scenario.situation: Win rate on deals created since the new sales script launched six weeks ago looks 9 points lower than the historical baseline (34% vs 43%), and the VP Sales wants to roll back the script immediately.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The VP Sales is convinced the new script is confusing reps and losing deals that the old script would have won.
scenario.question: Is the new script actually underperforming, or is something else explaining the gap?

decisions.prompt: The VP wants answers fast. How do you frame the investigation before touching the data?

options.label: Before/after comparison on the script launch date
options.detail: Split all deals into pre-launch and post-launch and compare win rates directly.
options.consequence: You confirm the 9-point gap — but pre-launch deals had months to close while post-launch deals are only weeks old. You've compared resolved outcomes to unresolved ones without realizing it.
options.divergenceCost: Anchored on the VP's timeline and compared cohorts with fundamentally different outcome maturity.

options.label: Diagnostic cohort audit
options.detail: Ask: are all deals in the comparison equally old enough to have had a realistic chance to close? Check the distribution of deal ages and closure status across cohorts before computing any win rates.
options.consequence: You immediately notice that post-launch deals are 6 weeks old on average against a ~90-day sales cycle. Most of them are still open — not lost. This flags a data-maturity problem before a single win-rate calculation is made.

options.label: Rep-level performance breakdown
options.detail: See whether the drop is driven by a subset of reps who struggled with the new script.
options.consequence: The rep-level analysis is noisy and inconclusive — too few post-launch closed deals per rep to draw conclusions. You've spent time on a dead end while the real issue stays hidden.
options.divergenceCost: Drilled into rep performance before validating that the outcome metric itself was trustworthy.

options.label: Regression model controlling for deal size, industry, and rep tenure
options.detail: Build a multivariate model to isolate the script's effect.
options.consequence: Your model controls for observable deal attributes but still trains on the same immature post-launch cohort. It produces a confident-looking coefficient for the script that is actually measuring fast losses vs. unresolved deals.
options.divergenceCost: Applied sophisticated modeling to a fundamentally biased outcome variable — garbage in, garbage out.

decisions.prompt: Your audit confirms most post-launch deals are still open. Now you need the right metric to test whether script performance truly differs. Which view do you trust?

artifact.title: Win rate by cohort — all deals created in each period
artifact.caption: Raw win rates across all deals. The new-script cohort looks 9 pts lower — but nearly 70% of those deals are still open and excluded from the numerator.

options.label: Raw win rate across all deals in each period
options.detail: Use the standard win-rate formula (closed-won ÷ total closed) applied to each calendar cohort.
options.consequence: The gap looks real and damning. But you're dividing by only the deals that have resolved — and post-launch deals resolve almost exclusively as fast losses so far. The wins are still in flight, invisible to this metric.
options.divergenceCost: Trusted a metric computed on incomplete outcomes, making the new cohort look worse than the data actually support.

options.label: Win rate restricted to age-matched, fully-seasoned deals (≥90 days old, closed)
options.detail: Filter every cohort to deals that are at least 90 days old AND have a closed outcome, then compare win rates on this apples-to-apples slice.
options.consequence: With the age filter applied, only 11 post-launch deals qualify as fully seasoned. Their win rate is 41% — indistinguishable from the old-script baseline. The 9-point gap vanishes when you compare like for like.

artifact.title: Win rate — age-matched cohorts only (deals ≥90 days old, closed)
artifact.caption: Restricted to fully-seasoned deals, the new-script cohort performs in line with historical rates. The apparent gap was entirely an artifact of outcome immaturity.

decisions.prompt: Age-matched win rates show no difference, but the new-script cohort has only 11 qualifying deals. What do you tell the VP Sales?

options.label: "The new script is fine — the 9-point drop is a data artifact. No rollback needed."
options.detail: Make the definitive call and recommend holding the script.
options.consequence: You're directionally right, but 11 deals is a very thin evidential base for a definitive conclusion. If the VP pushes back or the script really does have a subtle problem, you've burned credibility by overclaiming certainty from a small sample.
options.divergenceCost: Overclaimed certainty from a sample of 11 — correct diagnosis, but unsupported confidence level.

options.label: "The gap appears to be right-censoring, not script quality — age-matched data shows no difference — but the sample is small. Hold the rollback and re-evaluate in 6 weeks when ~60 more deals mature."
options.detail: Present the finding, name the statistical limitation, and propose a concrete re-measurement date.
options.consequence: The VP understands why the metric was misleading, trusts the analysis because you've been transparent about its limits, and agrees to a 6-week hold. You've protected the script from a premature rollback while giving the business a credible checkpoint.

insight: The 9-point win-rate drop was entirely an artifact of right-censoring: recent deals hadn't had 90 days to close, so the only resolved outcomes in that cohort were fast losses, mechanically suppressing the win rate. Once cohorts were age-matched, performance was flat. The lesson is that measuring outcomes on entities that haven't had time to resolve systematically understates success — any conversion or win-rate metric must be restricted to fully-seasoned cohorts, or the signal is noise.
